sentences.text: The CMM Court dismissed the application under Section 156(3) of CrPC by order dated 7th March, 2024 and instead, directed the Petitioner to lead pre-summoning evidence.
Aggrieved by the said order, the Petitioner preferred a revision petition before the Sessions Court, which came to be dismissed by the impugned order.
3. The Petitioner/Complainant - Amarendra Dhari Singh, is a sitting Member of the Rajya Sabha from the State of Bihar.
He is engaged in the business of international fertilizer consultancy and possesses extensive experience, expertise, and goodwill in both domestic and international fertilizer sectors.
Mrs. Aditi Shivendra Singh and Mrs. Arundhati Khanna (Respondent Nos. 2 and 3) are the nieces of the Petitioner, while Mrs. Rajshree Singh (Respondent No. 4) is his sister-in-law.

M/s R.C.
Nursery Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 5) is a private company in which Respondent Nos. 3 and 4 are Directors.

4. The case of the Petitioner, in brief, is as follows:
4.1.
It is alleged that around 29th/30th August, 2020, Mrs. Aditi and Mrs. Arundhati approached the Petitioner seeking financial help, claiming to be suffering from financial hardships and difficulties.

Despite the Petitioner's denial, Mrs. Aditi kept on insisting on the funds and proposed to sell a property belonging to M/s R.C. Nursery Pvt. Ltd., located at R-10, Maulsari Avenue, Westend Green Farms, Rajokri, New Delhi-110038, in lieu of the money to be taken from the Petitioner.
4.2. The Petitioner allegedly assured that the property was free from all encumbrances and that all taxes have been duly paid.

When the Petitioner expressed willingness to consider Mrs. Aditi's proposal, she offered to sell :IPC"

Relying on her assurances - and given his longstanding personal relationship with her father - the Petitioner trusted her and transferred a sum of INR 24,75,000/- to M/s R.C. Nursery Pvt. Ltd.

4.5. Subsequently, Respondent Nos. 2 to 4 again requested for additional funds, citing urgent financial need.

On their repeated assurances of repayment within three months of the receipt of the amount, the Petitioner, over time, allegedly transferred INR 66,70,00,000 to Respondent No. 2, INR 6,90,00,000 to Respondent No. 3 and INR 5,00,00,000 to Respondent No. 4.
It is, however, alleged that the after receiving the funds, Respondent Nos. 2 to 4 have continued to refuse the repayment.
4.6. The role of Mrs. Rajshree, in furthering this conspiracy of fraud and cheating, is particularly significant.
Despite being a director of the company, she is alleged to have deceived the Petitioner by misrepresenting the property as being free from all encumbrances.

Even after having knowledge of the subsisting encumbrances on the property, she permitted Mrs. Aditi to offer it for sale and even authorized Mrs.
Arundhati to proceed with its sale to the Petitioner.
Acting in furtherance of their common intention and criminal conspiracy, the accused are alleged to have cheated and criminally misappropriated the funds entrusted to them by the Petitioner.
Although the Petitioner lodged a police complaint regarding the incident, no FIR was registered against the accused.
Thereafter, the complaint case was filed before the CMM Court.

"30.
Keeping the above facts and circumstances of the case at hand, in revision, the scope is very limited.
Moreover, the observations made by Hon'ble Apex Court in Sakiri Vasu (supra) are squarely applicable to instant case.

There is no ground to deviate from the remedy available to petitioner under Section 200 Cr.P.C.
31.
Undisputedly, the Magistrate can exercise his power under Section 156 (3) of the Code, however must not exercise and pass the order mechanically on the mere asking by the complainant.

These powers ought to be exercised primarily in those cases where the allegations are quite serious and evidence is beyond the reach of complainant or custodial interrogation appears to be necessary for some recovery or article or discovery of fact, which is not in the present case.
32.

In the present case, complainant/ revisionist is in possession of all the materials which are required to be produced in support his allegations and the identity of alleged accused persons is well known to the complainant/ revisionist.

The allegations as raised by the complainant do not appear to be of such a nature requiring custodial interrogation of accused persons or intervention of the State in the form of police investigation.
33. However, the allegations still may be proved by complainant before Ld. Trial Court through oral and documentary evidence in his complaint under Section 200 Cr.P.C.
As such, the complainant has specific knowledge regarding the incidents in question.
Even otherwise, Ld. Trial Court has not dismissed the complaint, rather directed to lead evidence.
Therefore, the complainant has all liberty to prove his complaint by leading evidence thereto.
No proper justification is given in the grounds of revision petition, for referring the matter to police for investigation.

The reason for not ordering the registration of FIR in the instant case by Ld. Trial Court are well founded and are duly reflected in the impugned order passed by Ld. Trial Court,
keeping in view of the law laid down while deciding the application in hand.
34.
After going through the impugned order, I find that Ld. Trial Court has not passed cryptic order.
The said impugned order has reasons which are not repeated here for the sake of brevity.
Those reasons were outcome of proper exercise of judicial discretion.
Accordingly, I find no discrepancy or procedural irregularities in the impugned order passed by learned Trial Court.
The complainant has also failed to establish any illegality in the impugned order."

Counsel for the Petitioner submits that the impugned order suffers from glaring errors and contends that both the CMM Court and the Revisional Court failed to consider several factual as well as legal aspects raised in the petition.
The complaint clearly disclosed the commission of offences under Sections 403, 406, 417, 420, and 120-B of IPC.

The Respondents executed several sham and bogus documents - including a fabricated Board Resolution, a false Chartered Accountant's certificate, and an application under Section 5(1) - during the subsistence of a stay order, with the intent to induce the Petitioner to part with a substantial sum of money on the false pretext of an imminent property sale.

These documents were not merely internal; they were acted upon by various statutory authorities such as the LAC/ADM, AAO, and the Tehsildar, thereby further misleading the Petitioner into parting with his hard-earned money.

8. It is submitted that both the Trial Court and the Sessions Court failed to adjudicate upon the existence, purport, and effect of these documents, and did not consider why the Respondents executed such documents if the Petitioner had only extended a friendly loan.

The Respondents'
claim that the payments were made in pursuance of a friendly loan is belied by their conduct in executing these documents to gain the Petitioner's trust, which clearly demonstrates their premeditated mala fide intent to induce the Petitioner from the very inception.

It is further submitted that the mere absence of a sale deed does not preclude the commission of offences under Sections 420 and 403 of IPC, particularly when the facts, read in conjunction with the documents executed, establish the existence of an underlying sale transaction and the steps taken by both parties in that regard.
The sham and bogus documents were of such nature that even statutory This is a digitally signed order.
The authenticity of the order can be re-verified from Delhi High Court Order Portal by scanning the QR code shown above.
The Order is downloaded from the DHC Server on 18/07/2025 at 22:16:40 authorities were misled into acting upon them.
A strictly hyper-technical approach to the facts may be justified at the stage of trial, but not at the stage of investigation.
For the purposes of considering an application under Section 156(3) CrPC, the test is merely that of a prima facie case.

9. It is, thus, argued that registration of an FIR is necessary in view of the serious allegations of criminal conspiracy, cheating, and misappropriation of funds amounting to approximately INR 103 Crores, which necessitate a full-fledged police investigation.

Despite a prima facie disclosure of cognizable offences, as mandated in Lalita Kumari v. State of Uttar Pradesh6, the Sessions Court erroneously declined the request for investigation, relying solely on the familial ties between the parties and the existence of secondary evidence for some of the documents.

Additional District Magistrate/Land Acquisition Officer, and Assistant Acquisition Officer.

10. Lastly, it is submitted that the procedure under Section 200 CrPC is inherently inadequate to address the complexities of the financial fraud This is a digitally signed order.

The Order is downloaded from the DHC Server on 18/07/2025 at 22:16:40 involved in the present case.

A comprehensive police investigation is indispensable for freezing accounts, verifying the sham documents, and tracing the misappropriated funds - none of which can be effectively achieved without registration of an FIR.
11. The Court has considered the aforementioned contentions but remains unpersuaded.
The law relating to the registration of an FIR by issuing directions under Section 156(3) of the CrPC is well settled.

Indeed, the said provision empowers the Magistrate to direct the police to conduct an investigation in cases where it is found that the police have either failed to investigate the matter or have not conducted the investigation satisfactorily.
Such investigation may also be monitored by the Magistrate.

12. In Sukwasi v. State of Uttar Pradesh7, the Court observed that applications under Section 156(3)
of CrPC, are being filed in large numbers.

entities.text: Sukwasi v. State of Uttar Pradesh7
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Court emphasized that the provision should be used sparingly and only in unusual or extraordinary situations, where there is a miscarriage of justice warranting a direction to the police to register a case.
The Court further noted that since an alternative remedy of filing a complaint under Section 200 of CrPC exists, recourse to Section 156(3)
should not ordinarily be permitted.

It was clarified that there is no legal mandate requiring a Magistrate to allow an application under Section 156(3) CrPC; the Magistrate retains the discretion to allow or reject such an application.
13.
This position was reaffirmed in Ravindra Kumar v. State (Govt. of NCT of Delhi) & Anr.8, where the Court reiterated that Section 156(3) CrPC is a discretionary provision.

The Court stressed that the Magistrate must apply his judicial mind and may direct investigation only when satisfied that the complaint discloses cognizable offences and that a police investigation is necessary to gather evidence that the complainant cannot obtain independently.
Thus, a complainant does not enjoy an unfettered right to seek a direction under Section 156(3) in every case.

sentences.text: The Supreme Court, in Sakiri Vasu v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.9, further clarified the procedural safeguards available to an aggrieved person in such cases.

entities.text: Sakiri Vasu v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.9
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It held that where an FIR is not registered by the concerned police station, the first remedy lies in approaching the Superintendent of Police under Section 154(3) of CrPC or any another competent officer under Section 36 of CrPC.

If the grievance remains unresolved, only then may the person approach the Magistrate under Section 156(3) of CrPC, instead of immediately resorting to a writ petition or invoking the High Court's inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 of CrPC.

The Court also emphasized that the complainant continues to have the alternative remedy of filing a private complaint under Section 200 of CrPC, thereby reinforcing the view that recourse to Section 156(3)
must be exercised judiciously and as a matter of exception rather than rule.

15. In light of the foregoing legal principles, which have been duly considered by the Sessions Court,
the decision of the Trial Court - confirmed by the Revisional Court - that registration of the FIR is not necessary, in the opinion of this Court, cannot be faulted.

16.

The nature of the transactions, as alleged, does not warrant a criminal investigation, especially when the Petitioner is fully aware of the facts and has personal knowledge of the transactions in question.
Moreover, the Petitioner is already in possession of all the documents on which he bases his allegations of cheating.
Therefore, in the considered opinion of this Court, a police investigation is not required.

17. It must be emphasised that while the Magistrate is empowered to exercise its powers under Section 156(3) of CrPC, such power must not be invoked mechanically at the mere instance of the complainant.

These powers are to be exercised primarily in cases involving serious allegations where the evidence is beyond the reach of the complainant, or where custodial interrogation is necessary for recovery of an article or discovery of facts.
Such circumstances are not discernible in the facts of the present case.

18. In light of the above observations, this Court finds no reason to invoke its inherent jurisdiction under Section 528 of BNSS (corresponding to Section 482 of CrPC) to interfere with the revisional order passed by the Sessions Court.
19. Accordingly, the present petition is dismissed along with pending application(s).
